caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 261 of 1993
lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Additional Attorney-General, instructed by Md Sajjadul Huq, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioners. . 
Not represented ----- The Respondent.
parties:
Government of Bangladesh and ors ------ Petitioners 
vs
Hussain Muhammad Ershad ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The writ-petitioner, Hussain Mohammad Ershad, former President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, challenged the legality of the action of locking, up and sealing of the room of a house at 21 A of Jahangir Road, Dhaka Cantonment by the respondent No. 2, officer-in charge of the Cantonment Police Station, Cantonment, Dhaka, in the writ petition filed under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh stating, inter alia, that he on 6-12-1990 resigned voluntarily from the office of the President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and that on 12-12- 1990 when he was removed to Gulshan Sub-jail from his residence in Sena Bhaban the Government formed an Inventory Committee and that he authorized his brother-in-law Mr Mustafizur Rahman to receive his personal belongings from the said committee Mr Mustafizur Rahman received those belongings from the Inventory Committee on identification by the Committee and that Mr Mustafizur Rahman stored those articles with some of his own belongings in the rented house where a family was allowed to live as caretaker and a guard was posted there and that a Toyota jeep, not belonging to the petitioner, was handed over in the Jimma of Mr Mustafizur Rahman by the said Committee which he kept in the garage of that house under lock and key and that the petitioner was convicted in Special Case Nos. 7 and 60 of 1991 and was sentenced to suffer 3 years and 10 years imprisonment respectively and that against which orders appeals of the petitioners were pending hearing, On 7-5-1992 a police force led by respondent No. 2 raided the house and broke open the door of the house without any warrant or notice and entered into the room where those articles were stored and thereafter locked the room and sealed the locks and took away the jeep and that they evicted the family living in the said house and that against such acts the petitioner on 19-5-1992 filed a petition unsuccessfully in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate praying for unlocking the house but no order of search warrant and seizure was available on the record. 

 5. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Additional Attorney-General submits that there being no violation of any fundamental right of the petitioner the learned Judges of the High Court Division fell in error in law in directing to hand over the seized articles and the jeep, admittedly not being owned by the petitioner or Mr Mustafizur Rahman, in view of the pendency of Criminal Appeals against the orders of conviction and sentence passed in the Special Cases against the petitioner and there being no inventory before the court. In the instant case there is nothing on record to show that warrant for search or raid of the house was ever issued by any competent court under section 96 CrPC. 

 6. The submissions of the learned Additional Attorney-General that by such acts no fundamental right of the petitioner has been violated is misconceived. True, a search by itself does not operate as a total restriction on the right of a citizen to hold and enjoy his property, and as such action is a temporary measure for a limited purpose of investigation and interferes with the right of citizen to be secured in his home against entry, search and seizure, provided such acts are conducted and done in a lawful manner. In the instant case the raid conducted and the articles seized belonging to the petitioner is not only unlawful but equally are violative of Article 43(a) of our Constitution which provides, amongst other, that a citizen has a right to be secured in his  home against entry: search and seizure. Such right is a fundamental right of the citizen and is subject to reasonable restriction imposed by law. Search conducted with a duly issued search warrant by a competent court under section 96 CrPC is a reasonable restriction on the rights enumerated in Article 43(a) of the Constitution. But without complying with the requirement of section 96 CrPC no such restriction on the right of a citizen can be imposed. Thus the submission that by search and seizure no fundamental right of the petitioner is violated is misconceived on the facts of the instant case. The learned Judges of the High Court Division rightly directed the respondents to hand over the seized articles including the jeep.
